title: Fixed fee vs. contingency fee for R&D tax credits: which is better?
description: A fixed fee is the lower-conflict choice for most companies claiming the federal R&D credit; contingency fees face Circular 230 and AICPA limits.
summary: Fixed fee vs. contingency fee for R&D tax credits: for most U.S. companies claiming the federal research credit under IRC §41, a fixed fee is the lower-conflict choice because the adviser's pay does not rise with the claim's size. Contingency fees can cost less on small claims but face limits under Circular 230, AICPA rules and state accountancy law.

body.text: Fixed fee vs. contingency fee for R&D tax credits: for most U.S. companies claiming the federal research credit under IRC §41, a fixed fee is the lower-conflict choice because the adviser's pay does not rise with the claim's size. Contingency fees can cost less on small claims but face limits under Circular 230, AICPA rules and state accountancy law.
Prepared November 10, 2026. Statements labeled "Analysis" are interpretation, not statements of law. This report is not legal or tax advice.
1. Summary

Analysis: For most companies claiming the federal credit for increasing research activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §41, a predetermined fixed fee (or a transparent hourly fee) is the lower-conflict choice, because the adviser's pay does not rise with the size of the credit claimed. A contingency fee is not always more expensive, however. On small claims it can cost less than a fixed fee (see the worked example in section 5), and it requires no payment up front.

items: The argument that a consultant's fixed fee helps a client's research avoid the "funded research" exclusion of IRC §41(d)(4)(H) remains a misapplication. That exclusion concerns research the taxpayer performs for, or with money from, another person, not the fee a company pays an adviser to prepare its credit claim (section 3.4).
The official reporter citation is 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. 2014). The decision relied on Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (section 4).

Both bear on audit risk, which is central to the fee comparison. Section G is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and required, with limited exceptions, for tax years beginning after 2025 (section 3.5).

body.text: 2. The two fee models
2.1 Fixed fee

Under a fixed fee, the client and adviser agree a price for a defined scope of work before it starts. WiseTime's discussion of legal billing notes that fixed pricing encourages the professional to work efficiently, but that long or complex matters (for example, ones where new evidence emerges partway through) are not always a good fit. It also notes that a client may feel short-changed if the work finishes faster than expected.

Analysis: Because the price is set in advance, the adviser absorbs any overrun inside the agreed scope, which is why a clearly written scope matters. For an R&D credit engagement, the scope should state which tax years, entities and business components are covered, whether federal and state credits are both included, whether the work covers an original return or an amended return (refund claim), and whether representation in an IRS examination is included. Each of these drives the hours an adviser will spend, and each is a point on which a fixed-fee client can be surprised by a separate bill if the engagement letter is silent.

Analysis: A fixed fee is not automatically free of outcome dependence. If the fee is owed only when the credit is received, or must be refunded if the credit is disallowed, the arrangement may fall within the federal definition of a "contingent fee" even though its amount is fixed (see section 4.2). The label on the engagement letter does not decide the question; the conditions attached to payment do.
2.2 Contingency fee

Under a contingency fee, the adviser is paid a share of what the client recovers, and generally only if there is a recovery. Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) describes the legal-services version: in personal injury cases, contingency fees typically run from 20% to 50% of the recovery. Wex also notes that ABA Model Rule 1.5(d) prohibits contingency fees in domestic relations matters and in the defense of criminal cases. ABA Model Rule 1.5(c), as summarized by Wex, requires a contingency agreement to be in writing and signed by the client, to state how the fee will be determined, and to tell the client which expenses the client will owe; at the end of the matter the lawyer must give the client a written statement of the outcome. These are rules for lawyers, adopted state by state; they are not specific to R&D tax consultants, many of whom are CPAs or non-credentialed specialists governed by different rules (see section 4).

For R&D tax work, Myriad Associates (a UK adviser) puts typical contingency rates at 10% to 30% of the credit or relief obtained; its own conclusion gives a narrower 10% to 25% range. Myriad also describes hybrid models in which a modest fixed fee is combined with a success percentage of 5% to 10%. Acena Consulting's guide describes some U.S. firms quoting hourly rates capped at a percentage of the credit, typically in the 30% range, and notes that Circular 230 limits percentage-of-savings fees.

Analysis: Hybrid and capped-hourly structures do not escape the contingency analysis. A success percentage layered on a fixed base is still a fee that depends in part on the tax result, and a cap expressed as a percentage of the credit links the adviser's maximum pay to the size of the claim. Under 31 C.F.R. §10.27(c)(1) a fee is contingent if it depends "in whole or in part" on the outcome, so the part that varies with the credit is what matters.
3. Incentives and audit risk
3.1 The case for contingency fees

Wex records the standard arguments in favor: contingency fees let people who cannot pay up front pursue claims, they motivate the professional to pursue a good result, and they shift the risk of losing from the client to the professional. For an R&D credit client, the equivalent benefits are no up-front cost for preparing the claim and no fee if the analysis concludes that little or nothing qualifies. For a cash-constrained startup considering the payroll tax election available to qualified small businesses under IRC §41(h), that cash-flow point can carry weight.
3.2 The conflict-of-interest critique

The same Wex entry records the criticisms: contingency fees may encourage too many frivolous suits, may push lawyers to settle too early and for too little, and are often high relative to the risk the lawyer actually bears.

On a one-third fee, a lawyer who settles for $15,000 after about 10 hours earns $5,000, or $500 per hour, and the client receives $10,000. Holding out for $21,000 takes 30 more hours; the fee is $7,000 over 40 hours, or $175 per hour, and the client receives $14,000. The client is $4,000 better off with the larger settlement, while the lawyer's hourly return falls by almost two-thirds. The same article reports a study of Florida medical-malpractice claims by Eric Helland and Alexander Tabarrok (19 J. L. Econ. & Org. 517 (2003)) finding that time to settlement was 21% longer where contingency fees were limited.

Analysis: This evidence comes from litigation, not R&D tax work. The analogy is plausible in one direction (an adviser paid a percentage has a reason to finish quickly on small claims and to maximize the claimed amount on large ones), but no study of R&D tax advisers was found to confirm it. The direction of the incentive also differs: in litigation the concern is settling too low, while in a credit claim the concern is claiming too much. Both follow from the same feature, which is that the professional's pay tracks the dollar outcome rather than the quality of the work.
3.3 Why the incentive matters for R&D credit claims

Aprio states that claiming the R&D credit does not automatically trigger an audit. It lists possible triggers, including random selection or statistical screening, scrutiny of another area of the return, an audit of a related entity or counterparty, operating in an industry the IRS is focused on, exceptionally high credit amounts, starting to use credits after a period of net operating losses, and claiming a refund on an amended return, especially under the IRS's newer refund-claim procedures. It warns that an unsuccessful audit can lead to full disallowance of the credit and additional penalties.

Aprio does not list documentation as a trigger; it treats documentation as essential for defending a credit once a return is examined, advising that qualitative documentation be gathered early, alongside the quantitative support, because records become harder to collect over time through system changes, acquisitions and employee turnover. Aprio does not discuss interest. RSM US reports that the IRS's AI systems are particularly focused on R&D claims and that poorly documented claims can be denied; this is an adviser's commentary, and no IRS primary source describing such systems was located.

Analysis: Because the claim's size drives a percentage fee, a contingency adviser is paid more for a larger credit even when the extra amount carries more audit risk. The client bears that risk, together with any disallowance, interest and penalties. The accuracy-related penalty under IRC §6662 (generally 20% of the underpayment attributable to negligence or a substantial understatement) and the penalty for an erroneous refund or credit claim under IRC §6676 (generally 20% of the excessive amount) fall on the taxpayer, not on the adviser. Under a fixed fee the adviser earns the same whatever the credit's size, so there is no direct reward for stretching eligibility.
3.4 Correction: the "funded research" argument

That does not follow from the law. IRC §41(d)(4)(H) excludes "any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)." Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d)(1) provides that all agreements (not only research contracts) between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons are considered, and that amounts payable under an agreement that are contingent on the success of the research, and thus considered paid for the product or result of the research, are not treated as funding. Under §1.41-4A(d)(2), a taxpayer that retains no substantial rights in the research is treated as fully funded, and incidental benefits such as gaining experience in a field are not substantial rights. Under §1.41-4A(d)(3), a taxpayer that retains substantial rights is treated as funded to the extent of the payments received (plus the fair market value of any property received), with a pro rata allocation option where the stated conditions are met.

As noted in the summary, §1.41-4A is formally titled for taxable years beginning before January 1, 1986. Its paragraph (d) remains the operative funded-research rule for later years because the current regulations cross-refer to it, and courts and the IRS continue to apply it (for example, in Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, a Court of Federal Claims decision that analyzed the funded-research exception under §1.41-4A). The citation is therefore valid in substance, but a careful report should say it reaches current years by cross-reference.

These rules concern who pays for the research and who bears its economic risk. Analysis: The fee arrangement between a company and the adviser who prepares its credit claim is not an agreement under which another person funds the company's research, so it does not affect whether that research is "funded." The fee-model choice should be made on cost, incentive and professional-conduct grounds, not on §41(d)(4)(H).
3.5 Documentation rules that raise the stakes of an aggressive claim

Refund claims on amended returns. Since January 10, 2022, the IRS has required that a claim for refund involving the §41 credit include specific information for the claim to be treated as valid, following Chief Counsel memorandum 20214101F (October 2021). The requirement originally covered five items. On June 18, 2024, the IRS updated its "Research Credit Claims (Section 41) on Amended Returns" FAQs to remove two of them (the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the information each individual sought to discover), although the IRS may still request that information in an examination. The items that remain are the business components to which the claim relates, the research activities performed for each business component, and the total qualified wage, supply and contract research expenses for the claim year. The IRS has repeatedly extended a transition period during which a deficient claim can be "perfected" within 45 days after the IRS issues Letter 6426C or 6428; the IRS FAQ now states the transition period runs through January 10, 2027. Corporations filing Form 1120 cannot file an informal research credit refund claim and must file a formal amended return.

Form 6765, Section G. The current Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) includes Section G, business component information. Under the final Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, released February 2026), Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to exceptions (including for qualified small businesses electing the reduced payroll tax credit and certain filers with smaller amounts of qualified research expenses). The IRS had originally announced in June 2024 that Section G would be required starting with tax year 2025, then announced in October 2025 (IR-2025-99) that it would remain optional for 2025.

Analysis: These requirements matter to the fee comparison for two reasons. First, amended-return refund claims are exactly the category of filing for which contingency fees are most common, because Ridgely removed the Circular 230 restriction on them (section 4.3). They are also the category the IRS screens most closely at intake, and a claim that fails the information requirements can be rejected without reaching the merits. Second, the business-component detail now required on Form 6765 gives the IRS more information with which to select returns, which increases the cost to the client of an overstated claim. A fee model that rewards the adviser for a larger number therefore carries more downside for the client than it did when claims were reported in summary form.
4. The regulatory limits on contingency fees
It is directly relevant to whether a contingency fee is available for an R&D credit claim, and it has changed in practice since it was written.
4.1 The rule as written: Circular 230 §10.27

31 C.F.R. §10.27(a) bars a practitioner from charging an unconscionable fee in connection with any matter before the IRS. Section 10.27(b)(1) bars a practitioner from charging a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with any matter before the IRS, with exceptions in (b)(2) to (b)(4). The exceptions cover services in connection with the IRS's examination of, or challenge to, an original return; an amended return or claim for refund or credit filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving a written notice of examination of, or a written challenge to, the original return; a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties assessed by the IRS; and services in any judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code. Under §10.27(c)(2), a "matter before the IRS" includes tax planning and advice, preparing or filing returns and refund claims, and communicating with the IRS. The section was adopted by T.D. 9359 (72 FR 54540, September 26, 2007) and applies to fee arrangements entered into after March 26, 2008. IRS Notice 2008-43 added an interim exception for whistleblower claims under IRC §7623.
4.2 The definition of a contingent fee

Section 10.27(c)(1) treats as contingent any fee that is based, in whole or in part, on whether a position taken on a return or other filing avoids challenge by the IRS or is sustained by the IRS or in litigation. That includes a fee based on a percentage of the refund reported on a return or of the taxes saved, and an arrangement under which the practitioner will reimburse the client for all or part of the fee if a position is challenged or not sustained.

Analysis: Under this definition, a "fixed" fee that is charged only if the credit is received, or that is refunded if the IRS disallows the credit, may itself be a contingent fee, because whether it is owed depends on the outcome. A "no benefit, no fee" promise attached to a fixed amount is, in substance, an outcome-dependent arrangement.
4.3 Ridgely v. Lew and ordinary refund claims

In Ridgely v. Lew, 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. 2014) (Civil Action No. 1:12-cv-00565 (CRC)), Judge Christopher R. Cooper granted summary judgment to Gerald Lee Ridgely, Jr., a CPA, in a memorandum opinion dated July 16, 2014. Relying on the D.C. Circuit's decision in Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014), the court held that the IRS lacks statutory authority under 31 U.S.C. §330 to regulate the preparation and filing of "Ordinary Refund Claims," meaning refund claims filed after the original return but before any formal representation or adversarial proceeding with the IRS. The court reasoned that preparing and filing such claims is not "practice" by a "representative" within the statute. It declared the §10.27 contingent-fee restrictions invalid as applied to ordinary refund claims and permanently enjoined their enforcement. Accounting Today reported on September 30, 2014 that the IRS decided not to appeal, so the decision is final. (Accounting Today gives the ruling date as July 17, 2014; the court's memorandum opinion is dated July 16, 2014.)

Analysis: The regulation's text still restricts contingent fees for Circular 230 practitioners. Ridgely removed that restriction for ordinary refund claims, such as an R&D credit claimed on an amended return before any audit. The court did not otherwise address the propriety of contingent fees, and it did not address a credit claimed on an original return. Some commentators argue that after Loving, preparing an original return is also outside "practice before the IRS," but that question was not decided in Ridgely.
4.4 The December 2024 proposed overhaul of Circular 230

On December 20, 2024 (IR-2024-315), Treasury and the IRS released proposed regulations (REG-116610-20), published in the Federal Register on December 26, 2024 (89 FR 104915), to update Circular 230. In response to Ridgely, the proposal would remove current §10.27 entirely and withdraw the 2009 proposed regulations on contingent fees (REG-113289-08). In their place, proposed §10.51 would define as disreputable conduct, subject to sanction, both the charging of contingent fees in connection with the preparation of an original or amended tax return or claim for refund or credit, and the charging of fees that are unconscionable under the facts and circumstances. The proposed definition of a contingent fee, in proposed §10.51(b)(2), would cover fees based on a percentage of the refund or taxes saved, fees that otherwise depend on the specific tax result attained, and reimbursement arrangements that apply if a position is not sustained. Treasury's stated basis is its authority under 31 U.S.C. §330(c) to sanction practitioners for disreputable conduct, which it views as distinct from the practice-regulation authority limited in Ridgely.

A public hearing was held on March 6, 2025, and more than 150 comments were submitted. Professional bodies including the AICPA and NASBA generally supported a prohibition but asked Treasury to carry over the exceptions found in the AICPA Code; the National Association of Enrolled Agents urged that proposed §10.51(b)(2) be abandoned. Commentators have questioned whether the approach would survive a challenge under Loving and Ridgely. As of the most recent information located for this report (commentary published in mid-2026), the proposed rules had not been finalized; a company should confirm their current status before relying on either the current or the proposed rule.

Analysis: If finalized as proposed, the rule would reach the pre-examination amended-return refund claims that Ridgely placed outside §10.27, at least for Circular 230 practitioners (attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents and others who practice before the IRS). Contingent fees for representation after an examination begins would remain available. For R&D credit engagements, the practical effect would be to push credentialed advisers toward fixed or hourly fees for claim preparation.
4.5 The 2025 reconciliation bill provision that was not enacted

The version of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, that passed the House on May 22, 2025 contained a provision (section 112211 in the Ways and Means Committee text) providing that the Secretary of the Treasury "may not regulate, prohibit, or restrict the use of a contingent fee in connection with tax returns, claims for refund, or documents in connection with tax returns or claims for refund" prepared on behalf of a taxpayer. The AICPA wrote to the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means Committees opposing it, citing contingent-fee abuses in Employee Retention Credit claims. The provision was not included in the version enacted on July 4, 2025 (Pub. L. No. 119-21). Treasury's authority over contingent fees therefore stands where it stood before the bill: limited by Ridgely for ordinary refund claims, and subject to the pending proposed regulations.
4.6 AICPA and state accountancy rules

Circular 230 is not the only constraint. Section 1.510 of the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct (effective December 15, 2014; formerly Rule 302) prohibits a member in public practice from preparing an original or amended tax return or a claim for a tax refund for a contingent fee for any client, and from performing any service for a contingent fee for a client for whom the member performs attest services. Fees fixed by courts or other public authorities, and, in tax matters, fees determined by the results of judicial proceedings or the findings of governmental agencies, are not regarded as contingent. Interpretation 1.510.010 gives examples where a contingent fee is permitted in tax matters, including representing a client in a revenue agent's examination, filing an amended return claiming a refund based on a tax issue that is the subject of a test case involving a different taxpayer or on which the taxing authority is developing a position, and filing an amended return claiming a refund above the threshold for review by the Joint Committee on Taxation. The Code's examples state that a contingent fee is not permitted for an amended return claiming a refund that is clearly due because of an inadvertent omission.

Many state boards of accountancy and state CPA societies have adopted the AICPA rule or a similar one. The AICPA's comment letter on the proposed Circular 230 regulations noted that South Carolina has a more general prohibition based on its adoption of Circular 230, and that West Virginia permits contingent fees in tax matters only when the provider represents the taxpayer before a taxing authority. State rules vary and must be checked for the adviser's licensing state.

Analysis: Ridgely limited what the IRS can do under Circular 230; it did not change the AICPA Code or state accountancy law. A CPA firm that prepares an amended-return R&D credit claim on a percentage of the refund may comply with Circular 230 as interpreted in Ridgely and still breach its professional and licensing obligations. In practice this means the R&D credit advisers who offer contingency fees for claim preparation are often non-CPA specialty firms, while CPA firms more commonly offer fixed or hourly fees. A company considering a contingency arrangement should ask the adviser which professional rules it is subject to and how the proposed fee complies with each of them.

body.text: The sterling figures are UK market figures for relief administered by HM Revenue & Customs. The dollar range is Acena's general base-cost range by number of projects; Acena separately says internal-use-software projects take more time to document but does not give them their own range. All of these are adviser estimates, not official data. No federal agency publishes benchmark fees for R&D credit studies.
5.2 Worked example (hypothetical)
The figures below are hypothetical. It is not a market quote. For simplicity the same $8,000 fixed fee is used at every credit level so that only the contingency fee varies.

The break-even credit equals the fixed fee divided by the contingency rate: $8,000 ÷ 0.20 = $40,000. At 10% it is $8,000 ÷ 0.10 = $80,000; at 30% it is $8,000 ÷ 0.30 ≈ $26,667. Myriad gives a similar real-world illustration: a £100,000 claim might cost £20,000 in fees under a percentage model (20%).

Analysis: The comparison should also account for the cost of being wrong. If a credit is disallowed on examination, a client on a pure contingency fee that is refundable on disallowance may recover the fee, which is the risk-shifting benefit described in section 3.1; but that refund feature is itself what makes the fee contingent under §10.27(c)(1) and the proposed §10.51(b)(2). A fixed-fee client keeps paying the fee but has not paid the adviser a premium tied to the size of the claim. The larger the expected credit, the stronger the cost case for a fixed fee.
7. Conclusion

Analysis: Percentage fees reward the adviser for a larger claim, while the client carries the audit risk, interest and penalties that come with an overstated one. A fixed fee removes that link and gives a known cost. That makes it the better default for companies with mid-sized or large credits, for companies filing refund claims on amended returns (which face the IRS's information requirements at intake), for companies that will be subject to Section G reporting from tax year 2026, and for companies with low tolerance for audit risk. The answer is less clear for small or uncertain claims, where a contingency fee may cost less and requires no up-front payment.

The regulatory picture also favors fixed fees for most engagements. Circular 230 §10.27 still restricts contingent fees for practitioners except in the listed situations; Ridgely carved out ordinary refund claims, but the December 2024 proposed regulations would reinstate a restriction for pre-examination returns and claims through the disreputable-conduct rules, and the 2025 attempt to bar Treasury from regulating contingent fees was not enacted. Independently of Circular 230, the AICPA Code and many state accountancy rules prohibit CPAs from preparing original or amended returns or refund claims for a contingent fee.

items: Confirm whether a contingency or outcome-dependent fee is permitted for the return concerned under Circular 230 §10.27 as limited by Ridgely, under the status of the proposed §10.51 rules at the time of engagement, and under the adviser's own professional and state licensing rules.
Get the fee basis in writing, including whether any part depends on the credit being received or sustained, and whether any part is refundable if the credit is disallowed.
Confirm whether audit defense is included or priced separately, and on what terms.

For an amended-return refund claim, confirm that the adviser will provide the business components, research activities and qualified expense totals the IRS requires for a valid claim, and for tax years beginning after 2025, that the engagement covers Section G of Form 6765.
